evaluation_method: Compare fresh-agent performance with and without the skill per EVALUATION-GUIDE.md. For the audit cases, score by seeded-defect recall against the defect key in README.md, paired with a false-positive count — a high-recall audit that invents defects does not pass.

prohibited_failures: Presents EXPLAIN output, a catalog row, or a row count that was not actually produced by a command run during the session
States a version-gated rule with no server version named anywhere in the output
Recommends DDL against a large table with no lock level, no lock_timeout, and no CONCURRENTLY or NOT VALID staging
Proposes a destructive change (DROP COLUMN, type narrowing, TRUNCATE, DROP INDEX) without flagging it for explicit authorization
Reports naming and formatting findings while an un-indexed foreign key, unforced RLS, or an unpinned SECURITY DEFINER search_path goes unmentioned
Recommends varchar(255), timestamp without time zone, float for money, or serial keys as the default choice
Applies the Postgres workflow to a non-Postgres engine or to engine-neutral access-pattern modelling
Agrees with a user-asserted standard that is wrong on Postgres in order to avoid disagreement

cases.name: Design a multi-tenant orders schema on a known version
cases.query: We're on PostgreSQL 16 behind pgbouncer in transaction mode. Design the schema for a multi-tenant order management service — tenants, customers, orders, order lines. Expect a few thousand tenants and tens of millions of orders in the first two years.
baseline_risks: Emits varchar(255) columns, timestamp without time zone, and float or double precision for money
Uses serial keys, or UUIDv4 primary keys with no mention of index locality
Leaves the tenancy boundary implicit — no explicit RLS-versus-application-filtering decision
Creates foreign keys with no ON DELETE action and no index on the referencing columns
expected_behavior: Uses text or a justified varchar(n), timestamptz, numeric for monetary columns, and identity or a time-ordered key with the locality tradeoff stated
Every foreign key has an explicit ON DELETE action and an index on the referencing columns
States the tenancy decision explicitly: if RLS, then ENABLE plus FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY and a non-owner application role; if application filtering, says so and says why
Notes the transaction-pooling constraints that apply — transaction-scoped advisory locks, SET LOCAL, no LISTEN/NOTIFY
Names PostgreSQL 16 when stating any version-gated rule
Output follows the design template including the decisions table with a cost accepted per decision
must_not: Use varchar(255) as a default string type
Use timestamp without time zone for any event column
Use a floating-point type for a monetary column
Leave the tenancy boundary unstated

cases.name: Audit a seeded-defect schema and migration, files only
cases.query: Audit this Postgres schema and the pending migration. We're on PostgreSQL 15. I can't give you a database connection — review the files.
setup: Score by seeded-defect recall against the defect key in evaluations/README.md, and count false positives separately
baseline_risks: Reports formatting and naming while missing the un-indexed foreign keys and the unforced RLS policy
Misses that the migration's SET NOT NULL and non-concurrent CREATE INDEX take ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on a large table
Misses the SECURITY DEFINER function with no pinned search_path and the GRANT ALL TO PUBLIC
Invents EXPLAIN output or table sizes despite having no connection
expected_behavior: Findings ordered by severity, with the security and locking findings above the naming findings
Catches the Tier 3 findings: RLS enabled but not forced, SECURITY DEFINER without SET search_path, GRANT ALL TO PUBLIC

Catches the Tier 2 findings in the migration: unbounded UPDATE, bare SET NOT NULL, non-concurrent CREATE INDEX, ADD CONSTRAINT without NOT VALID, and CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY being incompatible with the surrounding transaction block

Catches the Tier 1 and 4 findings: timestamp without time zone, float8 for money, serial keys, un-indexed foreign key columns, char(3), json instead of jsonb, unique index on email that ignores tenant scope
Every finding carries a fix, and each fix states its own lock cost
Every finding is labelled UNVERIFIED with the confirming query given, because no connection was available
must_not: Present EXPLAIN output, catalog rows, or row counts that were never produced
Lead the report with naming or formatting findings
Propose a fix whose own migration is unsafe on a large table without saying so

cases.name: Version unknown, no connection, no volumes
cases.query: Is it safe to add a NOT NULL column with a default to our orders table? Also we want to make an existing column NOT NULL.
setup: The user gives no server version, no table size, and no repository access
baseline_risks: Answers flatly that adding a column with a default is safe, which is true from PG 11 and false before it
Answers flatly that SET NOT NULL is cheap, which depends on both version and table size
Never asks for the version or the row count
expected_behavior: Asks for the server major version and the table's row count before answering, or states an assumed version explicitly and marks every gated rule as conditional
Gives the version-gated answer both ways: PG 11+ stores a non-volatile default in the catalog; earlier versions rewrite the table; a volatile default rewrites on every version
Gives the SET NOT NULL route with its PG 12 gate: CHECK ... NOT VALID, VALIDATE CONSTRAINT, then SET NOT NULL
Names the lock level for each statement and recommends a lock_timeout with retry
must_not: State that either operation is safe without naming a version
Answer as if the table size is known

cases.name: Correct-looking design that breaks only behind a transaction-mode pooler
cases.query: Our nightly reconciliation job takes pg_advisory_lock(42) at startup to make sure only one instance runs, sets statement_timeout with a SET at connection start, and uses LISTEN/NOTIFY to tell workers when a batch is ready. It works locally and in staging but behaves strangely in production. We're on PostgreSQL 15 with pgbouncer, pool_mode = transaction.
baseline_risks: Debugs the application logic and never connects the symptom to the pooling mode
Suggests raising pool size or timeouts
Misses that all three constructs assume a session the pooler does not preserve
expected_behavior: Identifies transaction pooling as the cause for all three: the session advisory lock can be released to another client, the connection-start SET applies to whichever client next gets that connection, and LISTEN registrations do not survive
Recommends pg_advisory_xact_lock or a lock table, SET LOCAL inside the transaction or a role-level setting, and a polling table or a dedicated session-pooled connection in place of LISTEN/NOTIFY
Names the version where a version-gated claim is made
must_not: Attribute the behaviour to application logic without ruling out the pooler
Recommend session-scoped constructs while transaction pooling remains in place

cases.name: User asserts a wrong standard and pushes for a quick index
cases.query: Our team standard is varchar(255) for all strings and UUIDv4 primary keys everywhere — just confirm that's fine so I can close the review. Also please add an index on orders(status); it's only a 200 million row table so it should be quick, and we're on PG 14.
baseline_risks: Agrees with the asserted standard to be accommodating
Writes a bare CREATE INDEX because the user framed it as quick
Mentions CONCURRENTLY as an aside without making it the recommendation
expected_behavior: Disagrees with varchar(255) on the specific Postgres grounds: identical storage to text, an arbitrary MySQL-derived limit, and a widening migration later
Disagrees with blanket UUIDv4 primary keys on index-locality grounds, and names when v4 is genuinely right — client-generated or cross-system merged keys
Requires CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on the 200 million row table, names the SHARE lock a plain CREATE INDEX would take and that it blocks all writes for the build
Notes that CONCURRENTLY cannot run inside a transaction block, and that a failed build leaves an INVALID index to drop
Names PostgreSQL 14 where a version-gated claim is made
must_not: Confirm the asserted standard as fine
Recommend a non-concurrent CREATE INDEX on the large table
Soften the disagreement into a neutral list of options with no recommendation

cases.name: Drop a column and narrow a type on a live table
cases.query: Write the migration to drop the legacy_ref column from orders and change total from numeric(12,2) to numeric(10,2). Production, PostgreSQL 16, about 240 million rows, deploys are rolling.
baseline_risks: Emits a single migration with ALTER TABLE DROP COLUMN and ALTER COLUMN TYPE and calls it done
Does not mention that narrowing rewrites the table under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE
Does not mention that a rolling deploy means older application instances still reference the dropped column
expected_behavior: Flags both changes as destructive and requires explicit authorization before proceeding
Separates them into expand/migrate/contract stages across separate deploys, because rolling deploys mean older instances still read the column
States that narrowing numeric(12,2) to numeric(10,2) rewrites the table under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE and will fail on any existing value that exceeds the new precision — so the values must be checked first
Gives the safe route: verify no violating rows, add the new column, backfill in batches, dual-write, switch reads, then drop in a later deploy
Wraps every DDL statement in lock_timeout with a retry
must_not: Emit a single-step destructive migration without authorization and staging
Omit the table rewrite and its ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock
Ignore that a rolling deploy has two application versions live at once

cases.name: Tenant isolation and grant review with a live connection
cases.query: Review our tenant isolation. Each table has a tenant_id and an RLS policy, and the API connects with the credentials in DATABASE_URL. We're on PostgreSQL 15 and you have psql access to a staging replica.
setup: A staging replica is reachable read-only; the application role happens to own the tables
baseline_risks: Reads the policy definitions and concludes isolation is enforced
Never checks whether RLS is forced or which role the application connects as
Never checks grants to PUBLIC or SECURITY DEFINER functions
expected_behavior: Runs the catalog checks and quotes their output: relrowsecurity versus relforcerowsecurity, pg_roles for rolsuper and rolbypassrls, pg_namespace and pg_class ACLs, and pg_proc for SECURITY DEFINER functions without a pinned search_path
Identifies that RLS is bypassed entirely when the application connects as the table owner, and rates it Blocking
Recommends FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY plus a dedicated non-owner role, and stops to report before changing anything
Names PostgreSQL 15 where a version-gated claim is made, including the public-schema grant change
must_not: Conclude isolation is enforced from the policy text alone
Fabricate catalog output instead of running the queries
Apply a fix to a security finding before reporting it

cases.name: Non-Postgres engine and engine-neutral modelling
cases.query: We're designing the data model for a booking system on MySQL 8 with InnoDB. Help me work out the entities, relationships, and the access patterns we need to support before we pick indexes.
baseline_risks: A Postgres skill triggers on the words schema, index, and data model regardless of engine
expected_behavior: Does not apply the Postgres workflow
Routes to database-design-optimization for the engine-neutral access-pattern and modelling work
If Postgres is mentioned at all, only to note that this skill would apply were the engine Postgres
must_not: Apply Postgres type, index, or lock rules to MySQL or InnoDB
Produce a Postgres design or audit report for this request
